templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner its/their vs contractions
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By + -ing), passage-final blank; the agent is the right subject
items.passage: For centuries, the Haarlemmermeer, an expansive but shallow lake southwest of Amsterdam, repeatedly threatened neighboring cities and towns whenever powerful storms drove its waters across the surrounding lowlands. By pumping approximately 800 million cubic meters of water out of the lake between 1849 and 1852, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: three steam-powered pumping stations turned its bed into some 18,000 hectares of farmland.
the lake’s former bed became some 18,000 hectares of farmland, drained by three steam-powered pumping stations.
the conversion of the lake’s bed into some 18,000 hectares of farmland was achieved by three steam-powered pumping stations.
it was three steam-powered pumping stations that turned the lake’s bed into some 18,000 hectares of farmland.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something that pumped water out of the lake. Choice A places “three steam-powered pumping stations” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the pumping stations did the pumping.

B.why_wrong: “The lake’s former bed” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the lake bed pumped the water out of the lake.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the conversion,” so the sentence illogically says that a conversion pumped the water out of the lake.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: draining of the Haarlemmermeer, 1849 to 1852 (history of engineering). No named people. Band 6 as 188f7e3c (3.18): plain agent key, recipes W, N, E; key the shortest option.

band7.why: Target band 6, built on 188f7e3c: plain agent key after a By + gerund opener, foils W (lake bed), N (passive nominal) and E (it-cleft, dead per CB 2bca654a/dfbf5d33). No property or 'of' key, so not band 7.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Built from ...), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is the object, not its designer
items.passage: Through the early nineteenth century, lighthouses typically depended on curved metal reflectors, which squandered much of their lamps’ light. Constructed from concentric rings of glass prisms rather than a single thick piece of glass, ______ could redirect far more of a lamp’s light into one brilliant horizontal beam.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed a lens in the 1820s that
when French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed a lens in the 1820s, he made one that
the lens that French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel designed in the 1820s
it was a lens designed by French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel in the 1820s that
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes something built from rings of glass prisms: a lens. Choice C places “the lens” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the lens, not the physicist, was built from glass prisms.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the designer
A.why_wrong: “French physicist Augustin-Jean Fresnel” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Fresnel himself was built from rings of glass prisms.

B.why_wrong: The clause beginning with “when” follows the phrase, and the subject of the main clause is “he,” so the sentence illogically says that Fresnel was built from rings of glass prisms.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: the Fresnel lighthouse lens of the 1820s (science, history of technology). Band 6 as b369d54c and f0864217 (3.1): mid-sentence blank, the thing is the right subject and the person who made it is the main wrong subject; recipes W, S, E.

band7.why: Target band 6, as b369d54c: the thing (the lens) is the subject, its designer is the main foil; W, S and E (it-cleft) recipes. Each foil dies on 'Fresnel was not constructed from prisms'.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Relying on one another) with a dash aside, passage-final blank; the right subject is a compound of the two partners
items.passage: Each of the approximately 750 species of fig tree depends on minuscule pollinating wasps that crawl inside its enclosed flowers to deposit their eggs. Relying on one another to reproduce—the wasps breed nowhere else, and the flowers receive pollen from no other insect—______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the fates of figs and their wasps are thought to have been linked for at least 60 million years.
figs and their wasps are thought to have evolved together for at least 60 million years.
the shared evolutionary history of figs and their wasps is thought to span at least 60 million years.
it is thought that the bond between figs and their wasps has endured for at least 60 million years.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, interrupted by the aside between the dashes, describes things that rely on one another to reproduce: the figs and the wasps. Choice B places “figs and their wasps” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the figs and wasps are the ones relying on each other.

A.recipe: plural 'Y of X' nominal (P): the partners' fates
A.why_wrong: “The fates of figs and their wasps” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that fates rely on one another to reproduce.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the shared evolutionary history,” so the sentence illogically says that a history relies on one another to reproduce.

D.recipe: expletive opener (E), built on another noun
D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: fig trees and their pollinating wasps (science, ecology). No named researchers. Band 7 on 2bca654a (3.21): compound-agent key after an -ing opener with a dash aside.
band7_moves: compound-agent key on the 2bca654a frame: only the two partners together can rely on one another, and every distractor keeps both nouns but places another subject first
hardest distractor (A) starts with “the partnership,” the noun the opener’s idea of mutual reliance seems to describe, and keeps every fact
dash aside inside the opener (as 2bca654a) puts the participle 19 words before the blank; run about 35 words, 15 or more after the blank
the E option is built on another noun (“the bond”), not a cleft wrapped around the key; key is the shortest option

fixes: A changed from the singular "the partnership between figs and their wasps" to the plural "the fates of figs and their wasps": with "one another" requiring a plural subject, B was the only plural option and won on number alone

band7.why: Mirrors band-7 2bca654a: -ing opener with a dash aside, passage-final blank, compound-agent key, E and N foils. After the fix a plural 'of' nominal shares the key's number, so only the modifier logic separates it.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: possessive determiner before its plural antecedent, singular attractors in the previous sentence
items.passage: A male fiddler crab’s enlarged claw can account for nearly half of the animal’s weight, a burden it carries to attract prospective mates. Raising ______ outsized claws and waving them in approximate synchrony, dozens of males assembled along a tidal mudflat can resemble a single undulating organism, a spectacle that may help draw the attention of passing females.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The claws belong to the ones doing the raising, “dozens of males,” the subject of the main clause that follows the blank. The plural possessive determiner “their” agrees in number with “males,” indicating that the claws belong to the males.

A.recipe: wrong-number determiner (matches the singular crab of the first sentence)
A.why_wrong: The singular determiner “its” doesn’t agree with the plural noun “males,” the ones raising the claws.

B.why_wrong: “It’s” is the contraction for “it is” or “it has,” not a possessive determiner.

C.why_wrong: “They’re” is the contraction for “they are,” not a possessive determiner.

items.notes: Subject: male fiddler crabs waving oversized claws (science, animal behavior). No named researchers.
band7_moves: determiner before its antecedent (as 0bcb4417): the owner, “dozens of males,” is the main-clause subject 11 words after the blank
the previous sentence names one crab three times (crab’s, animal’s, it), so the nearest owner a reader has in mind is singular
two linked steps: each male has one enlarged claw, so “outsized claws” must belong to several crabs, the males of the main clause

band7.why: Determiner before its antecedent with 33 run words after the blank and three singular attractors (crab, animal, it) in the previous sentence, as 0bcb4417.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a long intervener of singular nouns, with a relative clause whose own verbs are singular
items.passage: The shortfin mako is among the ocean’s fastest sharks. The minuscule toothlike scales along the mako’s flank, each of which bristles outward whenever the water flowing over that region of the body begins to decelerate, ______ thought to function as flexible flaps that keep the flow from separating and generating drag.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the plural noun “scales,” so it takes the plural verb “are.” Everything from “along the mako’s flank” to “begins to decelerate” only describes the scales.

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with “each” or the nearest noun)
A.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “scales.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “scales.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “scales.”

items.notes: Subject: shortfin mako flank scales (science, biomechanics). No named researchers.
band7_moves: plural head (scales) 22 words before the blank, behind five singular nouns (flank, each, water, region, body), as dc645172 (3.3)
the intervener holds a relative clause on “each” whose own verbs are singular (bristles, begins), so the wrong number sounds right twice
the noun right before the blank (body) is singular; 15 words of the run follow the blank

fixes: explanation quoted "begins to slow"; passage says "begins to decelerate"

band7.why: Plural head behind a singular intervener with its own singular verbs (each of which bristles, begins), 15 run words after the blank, as 8a9d2f4e and dc645172.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two slots, plain plural then generic plural possessor
items.passage: The pangolin is among the few mammals clad in hard scales. Composed of keratin, the overlapping ______ backs and tails slide past one another as the animals curl into a defensive ball, an arrangement that engineers developing flexible protective armor have studied extensively.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The scales are many and slide past “one another,” so the plain plural “scales” is needed. The backs and tails belong to pangolins in general, as “the animals” later confirms, so the plural possessive “pangolins’” is correct.

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Scale’s” is a singular possessive, but the sentence needs the plain plural “scales”; nothing belongs to the scales.

B.why_wrong: “Pangolin’s” is a singular possessive, but the backs and tails belong to pangolins in general (“the animals”), so the plural possessive “pangolins’” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Pangolins” is a plain plural; the possessive “pangolins’” is needed to show that the backs and tails belong to the animals.

items.notes: Subject: pangolin scales as a model for flexible armor (science, materials). No named researchers.
band7_moves: two slots with a generic plural possessor and no article, as 2784cbaf (objects’ movement)
the number cues for the possessor sit downstream of the blank (backs and tails, “the animals”), and for the first slot in “one another”
option grid as 2784cbaf: needless apostrophe, singular possessor, missing apostrophe; key not the longest

fixes: first sentence made a singular generic ("The pangolin is") so B "pangolin’s" has an attractor, as "an object" in 2784cbaf; B stays wrong (bare singular possessor, plural "backs and tails", "the animals")

band7.why: Two slots, plain plural then generic plural possessor, as 2784cbaf; after the fix a singular generic opener pulls toward 'pangolin’s', with the cue 'the animals' downstream.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a three-verb compound predicate, against three -ing and finite forms
items.passage: Garum, a condiment made from fermented fish, seasoned countless dishes in ancient Rome. Following instructions in Byzantine agricultural texts, culinary historians layered anchovies and salt in earthenware jars, left the jars in the sun for about three months, and eventually strained the amber liquid through linen ______ an approximation of the sauce.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The to-infinitive “to produce” correctly begins a phrase that explains why the culinary historians strained the liquid: to make an approximation of the sauce.

B.recipe: wrong nonfinite: participle with no comma
B.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, the participle “producing” illogically suggests that the linen was producing an approximation of the sauce.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: Without a conjunction such as “and” before it, the finite past tense verb “produced” can’t be used in this way to add another action by the culinary historians.

D.why_wrong: Read as a verb, “producing” isn’t consistent with the past tense verbs “layered,” “left,” and “strained”; read as a participle, it can’t be joined to the sentence with “and.”

items.notes: Subject: re-creating Roman garum from old recipes (history, food). Unnamed culinary historians. No band-7 officials exist for R2_to_inf (band7 file, section 5), so written as a strong band 6 on 512f0ac9 (3.19): purpose infinitive after a compound predicate, three nonfinite or finite foils.

fixes: "strained off the amber liquid" became "strained the amber liquid through linen": comma-less "producing" read on "liquid" (the liquid that yields the sauce) was only odd; on "linen" it is plainly illogical, as "bacteria forging a tool" in 512f0ac9

band7.why: R2_to_inf has no band-7 official items (band7 file section 5), so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 on 512f0ac9 with a three-verb compound predicate and the comma-less -ing trap.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with an appositive full of plural nouns
items.passage: In the Andean city of Ayacucho, Peru, artisans have built portable altars known as retablos since colonial times. A typical retablo, a hinged wooden box crowded with miniature painted figures of saints, shepherds, and musicians, ______ an entire village celebration into a compartment roughly the size of a shoebox.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “retablo” (“A typical retablo”), so it takes the singular verb “compresses.” The phrase between the commas, with its plural nouns, only describes the retablo.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “compress” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “retablo.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are compressing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “retablo.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have compressed” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “retablo.”

items.notes: Subject: Ayacucho retablos (arts, folk art). Medium attractor: plural nouns inside the appositive (figures, saints, shepherds, musicians), as 2.21.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + adjective + plural noun, full grid
items.passage: Samoan writer Albert Wendt’s 1979 novel Leaves of the Banyan Tree is set in the fictional village of Sapepe. Spanning three generations of a single family, the novel chronicles the ______ as its members embrace, resist, or reshape the commercial values that arrived with colonial rule.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The fortunes belong to one family (“a single family”), so the singular possessive “family’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the fortunes, so “fortunes” is a plain plural with no apostrophe.

B.why_wrong: “Families” is a plain plural; it lacks the apostrophe that shows possession, and the novel follows only one family.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Fortune’s” is a possessive, but nothing belongs to the fortunes; the plain plural “fortunes” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Families’” is a plural possessive, but the novel follows a single family.

items.notes: Subject: Albert Wendt, Leaves of the Banyan Tree (literature). Number cues “a single family” and “its members.”

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: singular antecedent (a language) amid plural nouns
items.passage: Residents of San Basilio de Palenque, a Colombian community established in the 1600s by Africans who had escaped enslavement, speak Palenquero, a creole language found nowhere else. Since the 1980s, local educators have worked to keep ______ in everyday conversation among younger residents, many of whom grew up hearing predominantly Spanish.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to “Palenquero,” the language that local educators are working to keep in use. The singular pronoun “it” agrees in number with this singular noun.

A.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “them” doesn’t agree in number with the singular noun “Palenquero.”

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “those” doesn’t agree in number with the singular noun “Palenquero.”

D.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “these” doesn’t agree in number with the singular noun “Palenquero.”

items.notes: Subject: Palenquero, San Basilio de Palenque (social science, linguistics). Medium rival nouns: residents, Africans, educators, all plural.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: quantifier subject “each of” + plural noun and participial phrase
items.passage: Drumlins are long, streamlined hills shaped by glaciers advancing over loose sediment. In western New York, between Rochester and Syracuse, each of the approximately 10,000 drumlins left by the last ice sheet ______ in nearly the same direction, preserving a record of the ice’s movement.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular pronoun “each,” so it takes the singular verb “points.” The words “of the approximately 10,000 drumlins left by the last ice sheet” only describe “each.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “point” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are pointing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have pointed” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each.”

items.notes: Subject: the drumlin field of western New York (science, geology). Quantifier head as 2.23 (“Every last second of”), plural attractor drumlins.

fixes: explanation quote corrected to match the passage ("approximately", "left by")

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener describing a person, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: A proofreader at a missionary printing press in present-day Lesotho, ______ a retelling of the Zulu monarch Shaka’s life that was completed in Sesotho around 1910 but not published until 1925.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the novel Chaka was written by Thomas Mofolo as
it was Thomas Mofolo who wrote the novel Chaka,
Thomas Mofolo wrote the novel Chaka,
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes a person who worked as a proofreader. Choice D places “Thomas Mofolo” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that Mofolo was the proofreader.

A.recipe: passive that leaves the wrong noun as subject (V)
A.why_wrong: “The novel Chaka” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the novel was a proofreader.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “Thomas Mofolo’s novel,” so the sentence illogically says that the novel, not Mofolo, was a proofreader.

C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: Thomas Mofolo and his novel Chaka (literature). Recipes V, P, E (2.10 uses W, E and a dash variant); single-sentence passage.

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a habitual process, parallel present verbs
items.passage: Southern cassowaries, large flightless birds of the rainforests in New Guinea and Australia, swallow fallen fruits whole. As the birds wander the forest floor, the seeds of those fruits ______ through the birds’ digestive systems unharmed and are deposited far from the parent trees.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes something that regularly happens, using present tense verbs (“swallow,” “wander,” “are deposited”). The simple present “pass” is consistent with them.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “passed” isn’t consistent with the present tense verbs that describe what regularly happens.

B.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had passed” isn’t consistent with the present tense verbs that describe what regularly happens.

D.why_wrong: The past progressive “were passing” isn’t consistent with the present tense verbs that describe what regularly happens.

items.notes: Subject: southern cassowaries as seed dispersers (science, ecology).

items.subtype: Tense: simple present for a rule still in force (“still,” “can feed”)
items.passage: For more than five centuries, farming families in the Swiss mountain village of Törbel have collectively managed their alpine summer pastures. Under a regulation first recorded in 1517, each household still ______ no more cattle to the shared meadows than it can feed throughout the winter.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The word “still” shows that the rule applies today, and the sentence ends with the present tense “can feed.” The simple present “sends” is consistent with both.

B.recipe: simple past where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past tense “sent” isn’t consistent with “still” and the present tense “can feed.”

C.recipe: past perfect where the cue is present
C.why_wrong: The past perfect “had sent” isn’t consistent with “still” and the present tense “can feed.”

D.why_wrong: The past progressive “was sending” isn’t consistent with “still” and the present tense “can feed.”

items.notes: Subject: Törbel’s communal alpine pastures (social science, economics of the commons). The 1517 date is the attractor; “still” and “can feed” sit in the blank’s own sentence.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural object pronoun after “several of”
items.passage: In 1937, American painter Lois Mailou Jones took a sabbatical from teaching at Howard University to study art in Paris. There she sketched traditional African masks displayed in the city’s ethnographic museums, and she later arranged several of ______ in her painting Les Fétiches (1938).
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers to the plural noun “masks,” so the plural pronoun “them” is correct.

A.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “it” doesn’t agree in number with the plural noun “masks.”

C.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “this” doesn’t agree in number with the plural noun “masks.”

D.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “that” doesn’t agree in number with the plural noun “masks.”

items.notes: Subject: Lois Mailou Jones in Paris and Les Fétiches (arts, painting). Option set as 1.12.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head + appositive, be-family options
items.passage: In 1933, German psychologist Hedwig von Restorff found that people memorizing a list best recall the one item that differs from the rest. This tendency, now known as the isolation effect, ______ one reason that highlighting a key term makes it easier to remember.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “tendency,” so it takes the singular verb “is.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “tendency.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “tendency.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “tendency.”

items.notes: Subject: the von Restorff isolation effect (social science, psychology).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head + participial phrase, be-family options
items.passage: Potlatches, traditionally held by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast, ______ ceremonial feasts at which hosts distribute food, blankets, and other goods to commemorate births, marriages, and other significant events.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the plural noun “potlatches,” so it takes the plural verb “are.”

B.why_wrong: The singular verb “is” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “potlatches.”

C.why_wrong: The singular verb “was” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “potlatches.”

D.why_wrong: The singular verb “has been” doesn’t agree with the plural subject “potlatches.”

items.notes: Subject: potlatch feasts of the Pacific Northwest coast (social science, anthropology). Plural key as 1.7 and 1.28.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head + appositive, lexical-verb options
items.passage: In the Gnawa musical tradition of Morocco, the guembri, a three-stringed lute with a body covered in camel skin, ______ the hypnotic rhythmic foundation for all-night healing ceremonies, while other performers clap or play large metal castanets called qraqeb.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “guembri,” so it takes the singular verb “provides.”

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “provide” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “guembri.”

B.why_wrong: The plural verb “are providing” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “guembri.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have provided” doesn’t agree with the singular subject “guembri.”

items.notes: Subject: the guembri in Moroccan Gnawa music (arts, music). Verb provide, not set (set is also a singular past form).

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a fronted “When” phrase
items.passage: Sea pens are colonial animals related to corals, named for their resemblance to old-fashioned quill pens. When disturbed, many species ______ pulses of green light along their feathery branches, a display that may startle approaching predators.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “many species” needs a main verb, and the finite verb “send” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “sending” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

B.why_wrong: The participle “having sent” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to send” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: bioluminescent sea pens (science, marine biology). Canonical easy option set.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a subject with a prepositional phrase
items.passage: The zodiacal light, a faint triangular glow sometimes visible just after sunset or before dawn, is sunlight scattered by dust in space. Measurements from NASA’s Juno spacecraft ______ that much of this dust may come from Mars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “measurements from NASA’s Juno spacecraft” needs a main verb, and the finite verb “suggest” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “suggesting” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

C.why_wrong: The participle “having suggested” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

D.why_wrong: The infinitive “to suggest” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: the zodiacal light and Juno’s dust measurements (science, astronomy).

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + adjective + plural noun, two slots
items.passage: Indian artist Bhupen Khakhar was largely self-taught and spent years working as an accountant while he painted in his spare time. Many of the ______ depict ordinary tradesmen, such as barbers and watch repairers, absorbed in their work inside small neighborhood workshops.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The works belong to one painter, Khakhar, so the singular possessive “painter’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the works, so “works” is a plain plural with no apostrophe.

B.why_wrong: “Painters” is a plain plural; it lacks the apostrophe that shows possession, and only one painter is discussed.

C.recipe: needless apostrophe on a plain plural
C.why_wrong: “Work’s” is a possessive, but nothing belongs to the works; the plain plural “works” is needed.

D.why_wrong: “Painters’” is a plural possessive, but the works belong to a single painter, Khakhar.

items.notes: Subject: Bhupen Khakhar’s paintings of tradesmen (arts, painting). Structure as 1.16.

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an event earlier than a dated past event (“about seven months earlier”)
items.passage: In June 1629, the Dutch East India Company ship Batavia struck a reef off western Australia during its maiden voyage. The vessel, which ______ the Netherlands approximately seven months earlier carrying chests of silver coins, was bound for the company’s headquarters in Java.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The past perfect “had left” shows that the ship’s departure happened before another past event, the 1629 wreck, as “approximately seven months earlier” makes clear.

A.recipe: present simple where past perfect is needed
A.why_wrong: The present tense “leaves” doesn’t show that the departure came before the 1629 wreck.

C.why_wrong: The future tense “will leave” doesn’t fit a departure that happened before the 1629 wreck.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive “is leaving” doesn’t show that the departure came before the 1629 wreck.

items.notes: Subject: the Batavia, wrecked 1629 (history). Built on 1.24: earlier-than cue relative to a stated date; no simple past among the options, as in 1.24.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a complete clause
items.passage: Acorn woodpeckers live in cooperative family groups in oak woodlands from Oregon to Colombia. Each group may drill thousands of holes into a single dead tree or wooden utility pole ______ acorns throughout the winter months.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The to-infinitive “to store” correctly begins a phrase that explains why each group drills the holes.

items.subtype: Tense: simple past with a stated year
items.passage: Guinean writer Camara Laye grew up in Kouroussa, a town on the Niger River, where his father worked as a goldsmith. In 1953, while living in Paris, Laye ______ L’Enfant noir, an affectionate account of that childhood later translated as The Dark Child.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The simple past “published” fits the sentence’s reference to a specific time in the past, 1953.

A.recipe: present simple where past is needed
A.why_wrong: The present tense “publishes” isn’t consistent with the past year 1953.

B.why_wrong: The future tense “will publish” isn’t consistent with the past year 1953.

C.recipe: present perfect next to a dated past
C.why_wrong: The present perfect “has published” isn’t used with a specific past time such as 1953.

items.notes: Subject: Camara Laye, L’Enfant noir (literature).
